dockerfile.description: The images in docker/ are Dockerfiles named without the name or extension the default patterns look for.

packageRules.description: The npm lockfiles pin the CLIs the mobile release actions run beside a signing key, so a release waits the seven days n3oltd/frontend gives every third-party package.
Actions are pinned to their major tag, which the publisher floats to the newest patch, so only a new major needs deciding.
These actions publish no major tag, or one that does not follow their releases, so each is pinned to a full version and offered every new minor and patch.
One PR per base image: neutralise the grouping config:recommended inherits, so a fleet-wide image bump is reviewed on its own.
Debian publishes dated snapshots, which the docker versioning cannot read at all; parsing the date makes a newer snapshot of the same release an upgrade, and leaves a new release alone.

SQL Server carries its cumulative update in the tag, which the docker versioning reads as part of the name, so nothing after CU8 would ever be offered; parsing the CU restores that, holding the Ubuntu base steady.

n3o-caddy's final stage copies the builder stage's binary over the base image, so the two references must move in one PR; bumped separately, a half-merged pair ships a Caddy built against one version running on another. Grouped across the repo, which also keeps the estate on one Caddy.

The SDK build stage carries a two-component tag by design: it is discarded at the end of the build, and a repository's global.json floor can rise the moment a patch is fourteen days old, which a pinned tag only meets if something bumps it first. The runtime bases below it stay pinned, because those are what ship.

Umbraco 13 targets net8.0, and .NET does not roll forward a major by default, so a newer runtime base here is wrong by construction rather than merely undesirable: the image would build clean and fail at container start. Scoped to this file, because n3o-dotnet shares the package and should keep being offered new majors. A site moving to Umbraco 17 builds from docker/umbraco17 rather than a bumped copy of this one.
Umbraco 17 targets net10.0, so docker/umbraco17 holds its runtime base to .NET 10 for the reason docker/umbraco13 holds its own to .NET 8: a newer major builds clean and fails at container start.

The release listing yields directory names, so the trailing slash has to come off before the version can be compared. Raised above the default priority because prConcurrentLimit silently withholds new pull requests once ten are open, and with the dependency dashboard off there would be nothing anywhere saying a ResourceSpace release was waiting behind them.

ResourceSpace 11.0 is validated against the PHP that Ubuntu 24.04 ships, and a newer Ubuntu brings a newer PHP. Offering 26.04 here would produce an image that builds and then fails on a PHP the release has never been tested against. Scoped to this file so n3o-caddy and the rest keep being offered new majors.
LiteLLM publishes release candidates, nightlies and development builds under the same image, and supports only its latest stable release, which is the only tag of the plain vX.Y.Z form.
Zammad tags each build of a release as X.Y.Z-NNNN, which the docker versioning reads as a different compatibility on every build; parsing the build number makes a newer build of a release an upgrade.

pip_requirements.description: The CLIP service's dependencies are a Dockerfile asset rather than a project at the repository root.

customManagers.description: The shared Renovate workflow pins the Renovate image through the action's renovate-version input, which no packaged manager reads, so a release that hangs cannot reach every repository the day it ships.
The ResourceSpace release is a Subversion URL in docker/resourcespace, which no packaged manager reads.
